analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after breast cancer surgery.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate committee hearing or vote; it sat in committee from January 1997 until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar health plans and insurers from limiting hospital coverage after a mastectomy to less than 48 hours, or after a lymph node dissection to less than 24 hours. It also stops insurers from requiring advance approval for those stays, from paying women rebates to leave the hospital early, or from penalizing doctors who keep patients longer. A woman and her doctor could still choose an earlier discharge.
analysis.who_benefits: Women undergoing breast cancer surgery and their families, who would be guaranteed at least 48 hours of covered hospital recovery instead of being pressured out the same day. Doctors would also be protected from reimbursement cuts for following the minimum stay.

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans and insurers could not restrict covered hospital stays to less than 48 hours after a mastectomy or 24 hours after a lymph node dissection, or require plan authorization for those stays.
Insurers could not deny or drop a woman's coverage to avoid the requirement, offer her money to accept less protection, or penalize or reward her doctor based on the length of her stay.
The same minimum-stay rules would apply to individual (non-group) health insurance coverage, and a woman could still choose to leave early if her doctor agreed in consultation with her.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, which would bear the added cost of covering longer hospital stays; those costs could flow into somewhat higher premiums for all enrollees.

drawbacks.text: Mandating a minimum covered stay raises plan costs, and the bill allows insurers to keep charging deductibles and coinsurance, so some of the added cost would show up in premiums paid by all enrollees.

Many patients recover well and prefer to go home the same day; a fixed minimum could push care toward longer hospital use even when an early discharge with proper follow-up is medically appropriate, though the bill lets a woman and her attending doctor choose an earlier discharge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: women recovering from major cancer surgery would no longer face plan-driven pressure to leave the hospital within hours, and the bill was deliberately drawn to preserve doctor-and-patient choice and to defer to states that already required similar protections. The cost is a modest premium increase spread across all enrollees, making it a low-cost, low-risk patient protection whose main downside is a one-size-fits-all floor in a few unusual cases.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daschle introduced the Breast Cancer Patient Protection Act of 1997 in the Senate on January 21, 1997, joined by 14 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day.
A total of 22 senators cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats.
The committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plans that would have had to pay for guaranteed 48-hour post-surgery stays were better off because the bill never advanced. Women facing breast cancer surgery got no federal protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers who avoided the mandate

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Minority Leader and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in January 1997 and never reported it, held no markup, and gave it no vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats, and with the Republican-led committee taking no action, the bill never reached a vote where a bipartisan split could have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after mastectomy and banned cost-cutting tactics like early-discharge rebates and penalties on doctors who keep patients longer. Its defeat left their drive-through discharge practices unregulated at the federal level.
Guaranteed minimum covered stays mean more reimbursed inpatient days for hospitals performing breast cancer surgery. That benefit runs alongside the patient's interest in time to recover.
